description: Dillahunty cites the flood, firstborn deaths, Babel, hell, and Jesus’s temple scourge to challenge whether Knechtle can coherently reconcile divine wrath with love.
critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty directly tests Knechtle’s claim that loving wrath opposes harm by citing the flood, firstborn deaths, Babel, hell, and the temple scourge as apparent counterexamples requiring explanation. Principal limitation: The compressed catalogue supplies no textual context, conflates distinct divine actions, misstates Babel as destruction, and leaves “sentence everyone to Hell by default” doctrinally undefended, while sarcasm reduces charitable engagement. Live burden: He must show that cited victims are not relevant wrongdoers, establish morally comparable features across episodes, and defeat contextual reconciliations grounded in justice. Locked score: 77 appropriately rewards direct reply contact, concrete scriptural touchpoints, coherent counterexample pressure, and substantial relevance to divine-character tension, while withholding credit because evidential underdevelopment and rhetorical overreach prevent the catalogue from establishing incoherence.
